summary:
Legal gender recognition in Chile rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019. Adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery. People aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and the law does not cover those under 14, who are nonetheless recognised as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the "over 14 years old" wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, but the ruling applies only to that case.

Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. A bill criminalising incitement to hatred or violence on grounds including sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression passed the Chamber of Deputies on 9 January 2020; its subsequent fate is not sourced here.

Violence against trans people is documented and lethal. In 2023 Ever, a young trans man, was murdered by an acquaintance who dismembered the body and hid it for 24 hours; the killing is described in national reporting as Chile's biggest hate crime. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for nearly an hour at a Santiago hotel, the attacker telling the victim he wanted to kill him.

Institutional discrimination has also been litigated. In April 2025 Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros, alleging she was relegated to administrative tasks, that her private life was exposed without consent, and that support was denied to her.

Detention carries specific safeguards. Gendarmería's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation and rules on trans visitors' access.

Medical care is publicly funded. Sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy have been covered by the public health system since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to address and register transgender people by their social name. In June 2024 the Ministry of Health's Circular 7 suggested deferring initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, though the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by 7 votes to 3, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents.

Entry and protection on arrival are governed by the Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021, which bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 allows unrecognized asylum seekers to be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
A Chilean advocacy group's annual report judged 2024 a year of regression for LGBTQ rights, citing stalled equality and trans-rights legislation, the rise of the ultra-right and government inaction. Movilh, the Chilean LGBT integration movement, published its 24th Annual Human Rights Report on sexual and gender diversity covering 2025, and its achievements index records the campaign record behind the current framework, including the anti-discrimination law, inclusive 2012 census questions and the "El amor es amor" marriage campaign.

On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report by 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions. The report is a non-binding recommendation proposing to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors, and repeal Circular 812, which protects gender identity in schools. It signals legislative pressure on trans-specific care and school protections even where no binding change has taken effect.

Article 373 of the Penal Code, covering offences to morals and good customs, was historically used by police to harass homosexuals even for holding hands in public. A 2015 Movilh report noted that for the first time in seven years no police abuses against LGBT people were reported, credited to the Carabineros Human Rights Department. F&M Global Barometers publishes a country profile for Chile with composite scores on LGBT rights perception, including a specific Global Barometer of Transgender Rights index.
localsOnly:
Education protections are extensive and resident-facing. A Ministry of Education circular of April 2017, Rights of girls, boys and trans students in the field of education, requires schools nationwide to provide bathroom and shower facilities that respect the gender identity of trans students, alongside guarantees of social name use and gender-conforming uniforms, and non-compliance is sanctionable. It sits within a wider framework: the 2009 General Law of Education, the 2011 School Violence Law requiring Good School Coexistence Committees, the 2013 Superintendence of Education handbook ordering non-discriminatory treatment, the 2015-2018 National School Coexistence Policy incorporating the International Day Against Homosexuality and Transphobia into the 2016 School Calendar, and the School Inclusion law effective March 2016.

Law 21,430, published 15 March 2022, is the first regulation explicitly protecting LGBTIQA+ children and adolescents, including non-discrimination on sex characteristics and the right to develop gender identity, and obliges state bodies to create programs on sexual rights and diversity.

Support services for minors have shifted between ministries. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) through the 2026 Budget Law, while the Ministry of Health-run program continues providing support in medical centers. The Gender Identity Support Program Crece con Orgullo has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Since 2009 the National Organization of Gendarmeries has ended disciplinary sanctions against inmates that prevented them from dressing according to their gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the incitement bill after its passage through the Chamber of Deputies on 9 January 2020 is unresolved in the sources; no Senate or promulgation record is available here.

The Gendarmería protocol for trans detainees is reported as signed and as having a standing committee, but the sources do not establish whether it is published in full, binding nationwide, or accompanied by compliance data.

The outcome of Isabella Panes's discrimination suit against Carabineros, filed in April 2025, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

Whether Circular 7 of June 2024 remains in force, and how its deferral guidance interacts with the Medical College's position that physicians may still prescribe, is not resolved by the available material.

The practical reach of the Constitutional Court's April 2025 ruling on the "over 14 years old" wording beyond the single case before it is not established; the sources state only that the ruling applies to that case.

Whether the CEI 57 commission report's recommendations have been acted on in legislation is not sourced.
